etymology: From Geneva, the Swiss city of the Reformation, and psalter, a collection of the Psalms set for singing. Compiled under John Calvin between 1539 and 1562, with versifications by Clément Marot and Théodore de Bèze and tunes by Louis Bourgeois.
biblical_def: The Genevan Psalter is the great fruit of the Reformation’s recovery of congregational praise: the whole book of Psalms put into metre and set to sturdy melodies so that ordinary believers, not a clerical choir, might sing the Word of God back to Him. Calvin held that what God commands in worship He also supplies, and that the Psalter is the inspired hymnbook God Himself gave His Church. Thus the regulative principle of worship—that the Lord be approached only as He has appointed in Scripture—found living form: psalm-singing by the gathered people. Calvin called the Psalms “an anatomy of all the parts of the soul,” for there is no affection a man may feel that is not mirrored there, and so he labored to give every congregation the entire 150 in their own tongue. The tunes were dignified and unadorned, the harmonies kept simple lest the music eclipse the words. From Geneva this pattern spread through the Reformed and Presbyterian churches and shaped English and Scottish psalmody for generations. The Psalter teaches us that acceptable worship is not invented by men but received from God, that praise is to be God-centered and Word-saturated, and that the humblest believer’s voice, lifted in the words of David and ultimately of Christ, is a sweeter offering than any contrivance of human ingenuity. It is the regulative principle made audible.
webster_summary: A metrical version of the Psalms compiled at Geneva under Calvin for congregational singing, foundational to Reformed worship.
webster_full: GENEVAN PSALTER, n. From Geneva and psalter; the book of the Psalms versified and set to music under John Calvin, 1539–1562.
A collection of all 150 Psalms in metre, designed for the unaccompanied singing of the whole congregation.
The chief practical embodiment of the principle that God is to be worshiped only as He has commanded in His Word.
Its tunes, plain and grave, were intended to carry the inspired text without overshadowing it.
As the Psalmist enjoins, “Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him: talk ye of all his wondrous works” (Psalm 105:2).
scriptures: Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him: talk ye of all his wondrous works.
O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.
corruption_summary: The Psalter’s God-given pattern of reverent, Word-filled praise is displaced wherever worship is reshaped to please the worshiper rather than the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief modern corruption is the inversion of worship from a God-appointed offering into a self-centered “worship experience,” engineered for emotional effect and measured by how it makes the audience feel. The Genevan Psalter rebukes this at the root: Calvin asked not what men preferred but what God commanded, and answered with the inspired Psalms sung plainly by all. When the words of Scripture give way to vague sentiment and the tune is built to overpower rather than to serve the text, the creature has begun to dictate the terms of his approach to the Creator.

A related error treats the regulative principle as a relic and worship as a field for unbounded invention. But Nadab and Abihu fell for offering strange fire the Lord commanded not (Leviticus 10:1–2), and our Lord rebuked worship taught by the commandments of men (Mark 7:7). To recover the Psalter is to recover the conviction that God is jealous for His own praise, that He has not left us to guess how to draw near, and that the surest worship is His own Word returned to Him in song.
roots_summary: The Psalter grows from Calvin’s conviction that God supplies the very words of acceptable praise.
roots_lines: Calvin’s 1539 Strasbourg edition set the first psalms to metre and tune.
Clément Marot and Théodore de Bèze versified the French text.
Louis Bourgeois composed many of the grave, memorable melodies.
The completed 1562 edition contained all 150 Psalms.
Its pattern shaped Scottish, Dutch, and English Reformed psalmody for centuries.
usage: “The congregation rose and sang from the Genevan Psalter, every voice carrying the words of David.”
“Calvin grounded the Genevan Psalter in the regulative principle of worship.”
“The Old Hundredth descends from a tune of the Genevan Psalter.”

pos: n. (a proper name; an English Reformer and translator)
etymology: The surname of Miles Coverdale (1488–1569), English Reformer and bishop. The name is of northern English origin, from a dale or valley; Coverdale produced the first complete printed English Bible in 1535.
biblical_def: Miles Coverdale stands among the foremost laborers in giving England the Word of God in her own tongue. In 1535, building upon and completing the work of the martyred William Tyndale, Coverdale published the first complete printed Bible in English, supplying from Latin and German renderings what Tyndale had not lived to translate. He was no original scholar of Hebrew and Greek after Tyndale’s order, but a faithful and humble compiler with a gift for music in language, and his cadences fell sweetly on the English ear. His translation of the Psalms was carried into the Great Bible of 1539 and thence into the Book of Common Prayer, where for centuries English-speaking believers prayed and chanted the Psalter in Coverdale’s words—phrases such as “the valley of the shadow of death” that endure in memory still. Coverdale embraced the Reformation gospel, suffered exile under persecution, returned to serve as Bishop of Exeter, and again fled abroad in Mary’s reign. His life testifies that God advances His Word through ordinary instruments who count the open Bible worth poverty and banishment. The Reformers held that the Scriptures must come to the plowboy in his own language, and Coverdale’s Bible was an early and beloved answer to that conviction—a milestone on the road to the Authorized Version, and a monument to the doctrine that the Word of God is for all the people of God.
webster_summary: Miles Coverdale, English Reformer who produced the first complete printed English Bible in 1535 and whose Psalms entered the Book of Common Prayer.
webster_full: COVERDALE, n. From the surname of Miles Coverdale (1488–1569), English Reformer and Bishop of Exeter; of northern English place-name origin.
The translator and compiler of the first complete printed Bible in the English language, 1535.
His version of the Psalms passed through the Great Bible into the Book of Common Prayer.
A man who suffered exile twice for the Reformation faith and the open Scriptures.
His Psalter gave us “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil” (cf. Psalm 23:4).
scriptures: Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
corruption_summary: This entry faces little direct redefinition, though the principle Coverdale served—Scripture in the common tongue—is dishonored wherever the Bible’s authority is dulled.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Word of God belongs in the hands and on the tongues of all His people, and that its authority is not lessened by the simplicity of its messengers. Coverdale was no towering linguist, yet God used him mightily; the lesson is that the power lies in the Word itself, not in the polish of the translator.

What must be guarded against is the quiet downgrade that prizes the Bible as literature while doubting it as the very voice of God. Coverdale gave his life’s labor and twice his homeland for a Book he believed to be true, profitable, and abiding for ever (Isaiah 40:8). To honor his memory is to hold his Bible as he held it—inerrant, sufficient, and the lamp unto our feet.
roots_summary: Coverdale’s work rests on Tyndale’s pioneering labor and the Reformation conviction of an open Bible.
roots_lines: Born about 1488; trained as an Augustinian friar before embracing the Reformation.
Completed and published the first whole printed English Bible in 1535.
Edited the Great Bible of 1539, the first authorized English Bible.
His Psalter was carried into the Book of Common Prayer.
Served as Bishop of Exeter and twice fled into exile for the faith.
usage: “The cadences of the Prayer Book Psalms are Coverdale’s gift to English devotion.”
“Coverdale finished the labor Tyndale’s martyrdom had cut short.”
“Many of our most memorable Bible phrases were first cast by Coverdale.”

etymology: Popular title of Acts and Monuments (1563) by John Foxe (1516–1587), English Protestant historian. Martyr derives from Greek martys, a witness; the work records the witness of those who died for the faith.
biblical_def: Foxe’s Book of Martyrs, properly Acts and Monuments, is John Foxe’s monumental account of those who suffered and died for the gospel, from the early Church through the Protestant martyrs of his own age. Its most searing chapters record the Marian persecution, when Queen Mary I sought to drag England back under Rome and sent faithful men to the flames: Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley burned together at Oxford in 1555, Latimer crying, “Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man; we shall this day light such a candle, by God’s grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out”; and Thomas Cranmer, who in 1556 thrust into the fire first the hand that had signed his recantation. Foxe wrote not to glory in blood but to honor faithful witness unto death and to fortify the living against the day of trial. The book taught generations of English-speaking Christians that the truth of the gospel is worth dying for, that the Lord upholds His own in the fire, and that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church. It stands as a perpetual testimony against the persecuting power of Rome and a summons to the courage of confession. Scripture itself crowns this theme: the martyrs under the altar cry out, and they overcome by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, loving not their lives unto the death. Foxe simply added England’s names to that ancient roll.
webster_summary: John Foxe’s Acts and Monuments (1563), recording the sufferings of Christian martyrs, especially the Protestants burned under Mary I.
webster_full: FOXE’S BOOK OF MARTYRS, n. Popular title of Acts and Monuments by John Foxe (1516–1587); from martyr, Greek martys, a witness.
A history of Christian martyrdom from the early Church to the Marian burnings of the sixteenth century.
Its central record is the death of Latimer, Ridley, and Cranmer under Queen Mary I.
A work written to honor faithful witness and to strengthen the living against persecution.
It echoes the cry of the slain in Scripture: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10).
scriptures: Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
corruption_summary: The clear witness of the martyrs is dulled wherever Rome’s persecution is recast as mere misunderstanding and the gospel they died for is treated as one option among many.
corruption_paragraphs: A common corruption today is to flatten the Reformation into a regrettable family quarrel, where the differences between Rome and the gospel are minor and the martyrs simply victims of an unenlightened age. Foxe will not allow it. Latimer and Ridley did not burn over trifles; they died for justification by faith alone and against the idolatry of the Mass. To pretend the issues were small is to spit upon their ashes and to deny the gospel they sealed with their blood.

A second error is the modern allergy to the very notion of dying for doctrine, as though conviction itself were the danger. But our Lord called His own to be faithful unto death (Revelation 2:10), and the saints overcame by the word of their testimony, loving not their lives (Revelation 12:11). To recover Foxe is to recover the truth that some things are worth more than life, that the gospel is one of them, and that the candle lit at Oxford has not yet been put out.
roots_summary: Foxe’s work flows from the Reformation’s blood-bought recovery of the gospel against Rome.
roots_lines: John Foxe compiled Acts and Monuments in exile and after, first published in English in 1563.
Latimer and Ridley were burned at Oxford in October 1555.
Thomas Cranmer was burned in March 1556, recanting his recantation at the stake.
The book was widely chained in English parish churches alongside the Bible.
It shaped English Protestant memory and resolve for centuries.
usage: “He read Foxe’s Book of Martyrs and learned what the gospel had cost.”
“Latimer’s candle, recorded in Foxe, still burns in Protestant memory.”
“Foxe wrote to steel the living by the courage of the dead.”

etymology: From Latin institutio, an instruction or systematic exposition. The full title is Institutio Christianae Religionis, the Institutes of the Christian Religion, by John Calvin, first published 1536 and expanded through 1559.
biblical_def: The Institutes of the Christian Religion is John Calvin’s great systematic statement of Reformed theology, the most influential dogmatic work of the Reformation. Begun as a slim handbook of 1536 to defend persecuted French Protestants, it grew through successive editions into the magisterial four-book treatise of 1559, ordered around the knowledge of God the Creator, the knowledge of God the Redeemer in Christ, the manner of receiving the grace of Christ, and the external means by which God invites us into the fellowship of His Son. Calvin opens with the celebrated declaration that all wisdom consists in the knowledge of God and of ourselves, two truths so joined that neither is rightly known apart from the other. From that foundation he expounds the sovereignty of God, the ruin of man in sin, the unconditional grace of election, justification by faith alone, union with Christ, the work of the Spirit, the marks and government of the true Church, the right administration of the sacraments, and the regulative shape of worship. The Institutes are not cold scholasticism but warm, pastoral, profoundly biblical exposition, every doctrine anchored in Scripture and aimed at the glory of God and the comfort of the believer. The 1689 Confession and the whole Reformed tradition stand in their debt. To read the Institutes is to be schooled in a God-centered vision of all things—a theology in which the Lord reigns, grace is free, faith alone justifies, and the chief end of man is to glorify and enjoy Him.
webster_summary: Calvin’s Institutes of the Christian Religion (1536–1559), the foundational systematic exposition of Reformed theology.
webster_full: INSTITUTES, n. From Latin institutio, instruction; the Institutio Christianae Religionis of John Calvin, 1536–1559.
A systematic exposition of the Christian faith in four books, treating the knowledge of God, of Christ, of grace received, and of the Church.
The most influential dogmatic work of the Reformation and a fountainhead of Reformed theology.
A work both rigorously biblical and warmly pastoral, aimed at the glory of God.
Its theme is summed in Scripture: “That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection” (Philippians 3:10).
scriptures: Phil 3:10
That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death;
Jer 9:24

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.
John 17:3
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
corruption_summary: Calvin’s God-centered system is corrupted wherever it is reduced to a caricature of cold determinism or set aside for a man-centered theology.
corruption_paragraphs: A frequent corruption is the caricature of the Institutes as a cold, fatalistic system fixated on predestination to the exclusion of grace and love. In truth election occupies a modest place in the whole, and Calvin everywhere writes as a pastor, anchoring every doctrine in the comfort of union with Christ. The slander serves those who would dismiss Reformed theology without reading it; the remedy is to read Calvin himself and find a heart aflame for the glory and goodness of God.

The deeper opposition is the man-centered theology that makes God a servant of human autonomy and salvation a cooperative achievement. The Institutes stand squarely against this, declaring with Scripture that of Him and through Him and to Him are all things (Romans 11:36). To recover the Institutes is to recover a theology in which God is at the center, grace is sovereign and free, and the creature’s whole wisdom is to know and glorify his Maker.
roots_summary: The Institutes grow from Calvin’s conviction that all true wisdom is the knowledge of God and of self.
roots_lines: First published in Basel in 1536 as a brief defense of the persecuted French Reformed.
Expanded through editions of 1539, 1543, and 1550.
Reached its final four-book form in the Latin edition of 1559.
Organized around the knowledge of God the Creator and God the Redeemer.
Became the systematic foundation of Reformed and Presbyterian theology.
usage: “He opened the Institutes and found not cold logic but burning devotion.”
“Calvin’s Institutes shaped the confessions of the Reformed churches.”
“The first sentence of the Institutes joins the knowledge of God to the knowledge of self.”

pos: n. (a proper name; a contemporary Reformed pastor and author)
etymology: Douglas Wilson (b. 1953), American pastor at Christ Church in Moscow, Idaho, within the CREC (Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches). The surname Wilson means “son of Will.”
biblical_def: Douglas Wilson is a living Reformed pastor who serves Christ Church in Moscow, Idaho, and has been a leading voice for classical Christian education, the recovery of Reformed worship, and a robust, optimistic postmillennial hope for the triumph of the gospel in history. He is a convinced complementarian, holding that God has ordered the home and the church with men in the office of headship and women in the honored and distinct calling of helper and mother, against the egalitarianism of the age. Through his founding of Logos School and the Association of Classical Christian Schools, his prolific writing, and his preaching, he has labored to rebuild a thoroughly Christian culture under the lordship of Christ over every sphere of life. Reformed believers may profit from much in his ministry while also weighing with care the doctrinal concern that critics have raised. Wilson was associated with the Federal Vision movement, a controversy of the early 2000s touching the doctrines of justification and the covenant. Critics within confessional Reformed circles charged that certain Federal Vision formulations blurred the distinction between the elect and the merely covenanted, and risked obscuring justification by faith alone—the very heart of the gospel and a point on which the 1689 Confession permits no compromise. Wilson has since distanced himself from the label and affirmed justification by faith alone, yet the episode remains a point of genuine doctrinal concern that warrants discernment. He is best received as a vigorous laborer for Christ’s kingdom whose ministry is to be tested, as all are, by the Word.
webster_summary: Douglas Wilson, contemporary CREC pastor in Moscow, Idaho, known for classical Christian education and postmillennial complementarian convictions, and associated with the Federal Vision controversy.
webster_full: DOUG WILSON, n. Douglas Wilson (b. 1953), American Reformed pastor of Christ Church, Moscow, Idaho, in the CREC; surname Wilson, son of Will.
A pioneer of the modern classical Christian education movement and founder of Logos School.
A convinced complementarian and postmillennialist who labors for the lordship of Christ over all of life.
A figure associated with the Federal Vision controversy touching justification and the covenant, a point of genuine doctrinal concern among confessional Reformed critics.
His aim is summed in the charge to take “every thought to the obedience of Christ” (cf. 2 Corinthians 10:5).
scriptures: Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
Deut 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Eph 5:23
For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
corruption_summary: The chief doctrinal concern raised by Reformed critics is that Federal Vision formulations associated with him risked obscuring justification by faith alone.
corruption_paragraphs: The point of genuine doctrinal concern is the Federal Vision controversy of the early 2000s, which touched the doctrines of justification and the covenant. Confessional Reformed critics charged that certain Federal Vision formulations blurred the line between the truly elect and those merely within the covenant community, and could obscure the cardinal truth that a man is justified by faith alone, apart from the works of the law (Galatians 2:16). Because justification by faith alone is the article by which the Church stands or falls, any wording that clouds it must be examined with the utmost care, and the 1689 Confession permits no compromise on the point.

In fairness, Wilson has distanced himself from the Federal Vision label and has affirmed justification by faith alone, and much in his ministry—his complementarian fidelity, his labor for Christian education, his confidence in the advance of the gospel—is to be honored. The proper posture is neither uncritical embrace nor reflexive dismissal, but Berean discernment: receiving what accords with Scripture, weighing what has been questioned, and testing every teacher by the Word.
roots_summary: Wilson’s ministry roots in Reformed conviction, covenantal optimism, and the call to disciple every sphere of life.
roots_lines: Pastor of Christ Church in Moscow, Idaho, within the CREC.
Founder of Logos School and a leader of the classical Christian education movement.
A postmillennialist confident of the gospel’s historical triumph.
A complementarian on the order of home and church.
Associated with the Federal Vision controversy, a point of doctrinal concern he has since qualified.
usage: “Doug Wilson’s schools helped revive classical Christian education across America.”
“Reformed readers weigh Wilson’s strengths alongside the Federal Vision concern.”
“His postmillennial confidence shapes his vision of Christian culture.”

pos: n. (a proper name; a contemporary emergent author)
etymology: Brian D. McLaren (b. 1956), American author and a founding voice of the Emergent Church, author of A New Kind of Christianity (2010). The surname is of Scottish Gaelic origin, “son of Lawrence.”
biblical_def: Brian McLaren is an American author and a leading voice of the so-called emergent or progressive movement, whose writings, including A Generous Orthodoxy and A New Kind of Christianity, have promoted a fundamental reimagining of the Christian faith. Under the banner of conversation and humility, the emergent framework recasts the historic gospel: the authority and inerrancy of Scripture are softened into a flexible narrative; the substitutionary atonement of Christ is questioned and even derided; the wrath of God and eternal conscious punishment are recast as unworthy of a loving God; the exclusivity of Christ as the only Savior is blurred toward a hopeful universalism; and the moral teaching of Scripture, especially on sexuality, is revised to suit the spirit of the age. This is not a fresh expression of the faith once delivered but a corruption of it, a different gospel which is not another (Galatians 1:7). Where the apostle thunders that a man is justified by faith in Christ apart from works, the emergent project dissolves the very categories of guilt, propitiation, and saving faith into a vague program of social betterment and an open-ended spiritual journey. The Church must answer such teaching not with hostility of spirit but with the clarity of Scripture: there is one gospel, one Mediator, one atonement, and one name under heaven by which we must be saved. McLaren’s influence is a summons to vigilance, for the most dangerous error wears the borrowed clothing of Christianity while emptying it of its saving content.
webster_summary: Brian McLaren, a founding voice of the emergent/progressive movement whose A New Kind of Christianity reimagines and corrupts the historic gospel.
webster_full: BRIAN MCLAREN, n. Brian D. McLaren (b. 1956), American author and emergent-church leader; surname of Scottish Gaelic origin, son of Lawrence.
A chief promoter of the emergent or “progressive” reframing of Christianity, author of A New Kind of Christianity.
A teacher who questions biblical authority, substitutionary atonement, hell, and the exclusivity of Christ.
A figure whose project the Church must name as a corruption of the gospel and rebut on biblical grounds.
Against such teaching stands the apostle: “Though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you… let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8).
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
John 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Acts 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
2 Tim 4:3
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
corruption_summary: The emergent/progressive framework McLaren champions is itself a corruption of the gospel, hollowing out Scripture, atonement, and the exclusivity of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the emergent or “progressive” reimagining of Christianity itself, advanced under the appealing language of conversation, humility, and a “journey of faith.” In McLaren’s framework the inerrancy of Scripture is loosened, penal substitution is mocked as “cosmic child abuse,” the wrath of God and eternal hell are recast as embarrassments, and the exclusive claim of Christ in John 14:6 is dissolved toward universalism. Strip these away and nothing of the saving gospel remains; what is left is moralism and sentiment dressed in Christian vocabulary. The proper rebuttal is not contempt but clarity: Scripture is breathed out by God and inerrant, Christ truly bore our penalty, hell is real and eternal, and there is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12).

Underlying the project is the postmodern denial of fixed truth, which treats every doctrine as a provisional story to be renegotiated. But Paul warned of a day when men would not endure sound doctrine but heap up teachers to suit their own desires (2 Timothy 4:3), and he pronounced anathema on any other gospel, even from an angel (Galatians 1:8). To recover here is to hold fast the faith once for all delivered to the saints, contending for it with the gentleness commanded yet without surrendering one article of the truth.
roots_summary: McLaren’s teaching roots in the postmodern emergent movement’s revision of historic Christianity.
roots_lines: A founding figure of the emergent church movement in the United States.
Author of A Generous Orthodoxy and A New Kind of Christianity.
Questions Scripture’s authority, the substitutionary atonement, hell, and Christ’s exclusivity.
Represents the progressive reframing of the faith under postmodern assumptions.
Stands as a warning of error clothed in Christian language.
usage: “Brian McLaren’s books gave the emergent movement its popular voice.”
“The pastor warned that McLaren’s ‘new kind of Christianity’ is no Christianity at all.”
“Against McLaren we confess one gospel and one Mediator.”

pos: n. (a proper name; a fourth-century Christian woman)
etymology: Macrina (c. 327–379), called the Younger to distinguish her from her grandmother Macrina the Elder; elder sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa. The name is of Latin origin.
biblical_def: Macrina the Younger was a fourth-century Christian woman whose quiet piety and steadfast counsel shaped one of the most remarkable households of faith in the early Church. The eldest child of a devout Cappadocian family already adorned with confessors and martyrs, she was the elder sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, two of the three great Cappadocian fathers who labored to defend the full deity of the Son and the Holy Spirit against the Arian denial. After the early death of her betrothed, Macrina embraced a life of singleness, prayer, and service, devoting herself to the care of her widowed mother and the spiritual nurture of her younger brothers. Gregory of Nyssa, who wrote a loving account of her life and of her final hours, calls her his teacher and credits her with turning the brilliant Basil from the pride of worldly learning toward humble devotion to Christ. She presided over a household ordered to godliness, where the Scriptures were loved, the poor were served, and the things of God were esteemed above the things of the world. In Macrina the honor due to godly womanhood shines clearly: not the seizing of office God did not appoint, but the high and fruitful calling of faith, prayer, hospitality, and the discipling influence of a holy life. Her memory rebukes both the worldliness that despises such hidden devotion and the rebellion that despises the order God has set, and it commends the beauty of a woman who feared the Lord.
webster_summary: Macrina the Younger (c. 327–379), elder sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, honored for her piety within the Cappadocian household of faith.
webster_full: MACRINA THE YOUNGER, n. Macrina (c. 327–379), of Cappadocia; the Younger, to distinguish her from her grandmother; name of Latin origin.
The eldest child of a devout family and elder sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa.
A woman who embraced singleness, prayer, and service after the death of her betrothed.
Credited by Gregory of Nyssa with turning Basil from worldly pride to humble devotion.
Her life adorns the praise of Scripture: “a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Proverbs 31:30).
scriptures: Prov 31:30
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.
Titus 2:3
The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;
1 Pet 3:4
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Macrina’s example is corrupted wherever godly womanhood is despised, whether by a world that scorns hidden devotion or by an egalitarianism that resents God’s appointed order.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption recasts a woman like Macrina as a victim of a patriarchal age whose true worth lay in opportunities denied her, measuring her by offices she did not hold rather than by the godliness she did possess. This egalitarian lens despises the very thing Scripture praises—the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in God’s sight of great price (1 Peter 3:4)—and treats the high calling of faith, prayer, and the discipling of a household as a lesser thing. The rebuttal is that God Himself crowns the woman who fears the Lord (Proverbs 31:30), and Macrina’s influence over Basil and Gregory shows how mighty such a calling truly is.

An opposite corruption is the worldly contempt that dismisses hidden piety as small and unremarkable beside public achievement. But the older women are charged to be teachers of good things and examples of holiness (Titus 2:3), and the Church owes much of its strength to women who, like Macrina, sought no spotlight yet shaped saints. To honor her rightly is to honor both the dignity of godly womanhood and the order God has wisely set, neither despising the woman nor overturning the design.
roots_summary: Macrina’s witness roots in the devout Cappadocian household that gave the Church its great defenders of the Trinity.
roots_lines: Born about 327 into a Cappadocian family rich in confessors and martyrs.
Elder sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa.
Chose singleness and service after the death of her betrothed.
Shaped her brothers’ turn from worldly ambition to devotion.
Honored by Gregory of Nyssa in his account of her life and death.
usage: “Gregory called his sister Macrina his teacher in the things of God.”
“Macrina’s household nurtured two of the great defenders of the Trinity.”
“Her hidden piety did more for the Church than many a famous name.”

etymology: From Greek allēgoria, speaking otherwise, and exēgēsis, a drawing out or explanation. The method is especially associated with the Alexandrian school and with Origen (c. 185–253).
biblical_def: Allegorical exegesis is a method of interpreting Scripture that seeks a hidden spiritual meaning beneath the plain sense of the text, often loosing the interpretation from the words and history actually written. It flowered in the Alexandrian school, above all in Origen, who taught that the letter of Scripture was a husk concealing deeper allegorical and spiritual kernels, and who frequently dissolved the historical narrative into figures of the soul’s ascent. While such reading could honor the unity of Scripture, it carried grave dangers: untethered from the grammatical and historical sense, the interpreter could make any passage mean almost anything, and the authority of the text passed quietly from the Word to the ingenuity of the expositor. The Reformers, recovering the conviction that Scripture has one true sense which is the literal or grammatical-historical sense intended by the Holy Spirit through the human author, rejected the multiplied medieval senses and the Alexandrian habit of allegorizing away the plain meaning. Calvin and Luther alike insisted that the interpreter must follow the words, the grammar, and the historical setting, and that the obscure must be read by the clear. Yet the Reformers did not deny genuine typology: where Scripture itself teaches that persons, events, and institutions of the old covenant foreshadow Christ—Adam, the Passover lamb, the temple, the brazen serpent—there the type is honored because the Word authorizes it. The line is plain: typology is taught by Scripture; allegorical overreach is imposed upon it. Sound exegesis follows the text where God has spoken and refuses to manufacture meanings He has not.
webster_summary: A method, associated with the Alexandrian school and Origen, that seeks hidden spiritual meanings beneath the plain text; contrasted with the grammatical-historical reading the Reformers recovered.
webster_full: ALLEGORICAL EXEGESIS, n. From Greek allēgoria, speaking otherwise, and exēgēsis, explanation; the method especially of Origen and the Alexandrian school.
The seeking of a hidden spiritual sense beneath, and often apart from, the plain meaning of Scripture.
A method prone to detach interpretation from the words and history actually written.
Distinguished from the grammatical-historical reading recovered by the Reformers, and from the genuine typology Scripture itself teaches.
Against forced reading stands the apostolic charge “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15).
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
corruption_summary: The chief error is allegorical overreach that detaches meaning from the text, against which the Reformers recovered the single grammatical-historical sense while preserving genuine typology.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is allegorical overreach: the Alexandrian and Origenist habit of treating the plain words of Scripture as a mere husk to be discarded for hidden meanings of the interpreter’s devising. Once the text is loosed from its grammar and history, no prophecy remains of its own determinate sense, and Scripture is made of private interpretation (2 Peter 1:20), the very thing Peter forbids. The remedy the Reformers recovered is the conviction that the Holy Spirit intends one true sense—the literal, grammatical-historical sense—and that the workman must rightly divide the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15) rather than impose his own ingenuity upon it.

Yet recovery must not overcorrect into a flat literalism that denies the typology Scripture itself teaches. Paul says the events of Israel happened as ensamples written for our admonition (1 Corinthians 10:11), and the New Testament reads Adam, the Passover, the temple, and the brazen serpent as true foreshadowings of Christ. The principle to recover is therefore exact: honor every type the Word authorizes, but refuse every allegory the Word does not, reading the obscure by the clear and following the text where God has spoken.
roots_summary: The method roots in the Alexandrian school and was answered by the Reformation recovery of grammatical-historical interpretation.
roots_lines: Flowered in the Alexandrian school, supremely in Origen (c. 185–253).
Sought multiple hidden senses beneath the plain text.
Multiplied in the medieval fourfold scheme of senses.
Was answered by Luther and Calvin’s recovery of the single literal sense.
Distinguished sharply from the genuine typology Scripture itself authorizes.
usage: “Origen’s allegorical exegesis often dissolved the history of the text into figures of the soul.”
“The Reformers traded allegorical overreach for the grammatical-historical sense.”
“Genuine typology is not allegorical exegesis; the one is taught by Scripture, the other imposed upon it.”

pos: n. (a doctrine of ecclesiology; church polity)
etymology: From church, Old English cirice from Greek kyriakon, belonging to the Lord, and government, from Latin gubernare, to steer or rule. The term names the manner in which Christ orders and rules His Church.
biblical_def: Church government is the biblical ordering of Christ’s Church for her worship, discipline, and edification, established not by human preference but by the appointment of her sovereign Head. The New Testament reveals Christ ruling His Church by His Word and Spirit through officers He has instituted. Scripture names two ordinary and perpetual offices: the elder, also called overseer or pastor, charged with teaching, ruling, and shepherding the flock; and the deacon, charged with the ministry of mercy and the care of the church’s practical affairs. The qualifications for both are laid down in the apostolic letters, and the offices are reserved, in keeping with the complementarian order God has set, to men called and gifted of God. The Scriptures further show a plurality of elders in each congregation, for the apostles ordained elders, in the plural, in every church, that no single man should lord it over Christ’s heritage but that the flock be shepherded by a council of qualified men under Christ. With this stands the congregation’s own responsibility: the gathered church is called to receive sound teaching, to exercise discipline, to guard the purity of her membership, and to honor and submit to her lawful officers in the Lord. The 1689 Confession sets forth this pattern: Christ alone is Head and Lawgiver of His Church, no man may add offices or laws He has not appointed, and the regulative principle that governs worship governs polity as well. Church government rightly ordered guards the gospel, feeds the sheep, and keeps the Church in subjection to her one true King.
webster_summary: The biblical ordering of Christ’s Church through the two offices of elder and deacon, a plurality of elders, and congregational responsibility under Christ the Head.
webster_full: CHURCH GOVERNMENT, n. From church, Greek kyriakon, the Lord’s, and government, Latin gubernare, to rule; the manner in which Christ orders His Church.
The ordering of the Church for worship, discipline, and edification by Christ’s own appointment.
Comprising two perpetual offices: elder (overseer, pastor) and deacon.
Marked by a plurality of qualified men as elders and the responsibility of the gathered congregation.
Founded on the apostolic practice: “And when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Acts 14:23).
scriptures: Acts 14:23
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
1 Tim 3:1
This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
1 Pet 5:2
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: Biblical polity is corrupted on one side by hierarchies Christ never appointed and on the other by disorder that despises the offices He did appoint.
corruption_paragraphs: One corruption multiplies offices and powers Scripture nowhere grants—the ascending ranks of prelacy and, supremely, the papal monarchy, which exalts one man as universal head over the whole Church. But Christ alone is Head of the Church (Ephesians 1:22), and Peter, far from claiming dominion, charged the elders to feed the flock not as lords but as examples (1 Peter 5:2–3). To add offices and rulers Christ has not appointed is to usurp His crown rights and to bind consciences with the commandments of men. The remedy is the plain New Testament pattern of elders and deacons, with no rank above the local eldership but Christ Himself.

An opposite corruption is the disorder that despises office altogether, whether the egalitarian rejection of the male eldership God has appointed or a rugged individualism that submits to no shepherd. Yet the apostles ordained elders in every church (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5) and reserved the office to qualified men, and believers are commanded to obey those who have the rule over them and to submit. To recover biblical church government is to walk between hierarchy and chaos, honoring the offices Christ instituted, the plurality of elders He ordained, and the congregation’s responsibility under His sole headship.
roots_summary: Biblical polity roots in Christ’s sole headship and His appointment of elders and deacons over His Church.
roots_lines: Christ alone is Head and Lawgiver of His Church.
Two perpetual offices are appointed: elder and deacon.
Each congregation is shepherded by a plurality of qualified male elders.
The gathered congregation bears responsibility for discipline and purity.
The 1689 Confession sets forth this New Testament pattern of polity.
usage: “Sound church government guards the gospel and feeds the flock.”
“The apostles ordained a plurality of elders in every church.”
“Biblical church government knows no head above the local eldership but Christ.”

pos: n. (a form of church government; congregationalism)
etymology: From independent, Latin in- (not) and dependere (to hang from), and polity, Greek politeia, the governance of a body. The term names congregational independency, in which each local church governs itself under Christ.
biblical_def: Independent polity, also called congregational independency, is the conviction that each local church is a complete and self-governing body under the sole headship of Christ and the authority of Scripture, answerable to no higher ecclesiastical court or earthly ruler. It holds that Christ has given to every rightly gathered congregation all the officers, ordinances, and authority needful for her own worship, discipline, and government, so that no bishop, synod, or pope stands over her with binding jurisdiction. This does not make the church a lawless democracy nor cut her off from her sisters; rather, she is ruled by her own elders under Christ, and she walks in voluntary fellowship and counsel with other true churches without surrendering her self-government. The 1689 Confession embraces this independency: it confesses that the Lord Jesus, as King and Head of the Church, has appointed a government in the hand of church officers distinct from the civil magistrate, and that each particular congregation is competent under Christ to choose her officers and exercise discipline. Against the prelacy that subjects churches to a chain of bishops, and supremely against the papal monarchy that claims one man as universal head, independent polity insists that Christ alone is Head and that His Word, not the decrees of men, binds the conscience. It honors the dignity Christ has given the local church, refuses the inventions of human hierarchy, and keeps every congregation directly accountable to her one Lord. Thus the autonomy of the local church is no proud isolation but a glad submission to Christ above every earthly authority.
webster_summary: Congregational independency: the self-government of each local church under Christ and Scripture, against prelacy and the papal monarchy.
webster_full: INDEPENDENT POLITY, n. From independent, Latin dependere, to hang from, with in-, not; and polity, Greek politeia, governance.
The principle that each local church is a complete, self-governing body under Christ alone.
Holding that no bishop, synod, or pope bears binding jurisdiction over the local congregation.
Practiced with voluntary fellowship and counsel among true churches, without surrender of self-government.
Founded on Christ’s sole headship: “And gave him to be the head over all things to the church” (Ephesians 1:22).
scriptures: Eph 1:22
And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church,
Matt 18:17
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Acts 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
corruption_summary: Independency stands against the prelacy and papal monarchy that subject churches to human hierarchy, and is itself corrupted when autonomy decays into proud isolation or lawlessness.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption independency chiefly opposes is prelacy and, supremely, the papal monarchy, which place over the local church a chain of bishops and at last one man claiming to be universal head and vicar of Christ on earth. But Scripture gives that headship to Christ alone, who is the head of the body, the church, that in all things He might have the preeminence (Colossians 1:18). To erect a human monarch over Christ’s churches is to usurp His throne and to bind the conscience with jurisdiction He never granted. Independency answers that He has equipped each congregation under Himself, so that final discipline rests with the church and her Lord (Matthew 18:17), not with a distant prelate.

Independency has its own besetting corruption when self-government decays into proud isolation, lawlessness, or contempt for the counsel of sister churches. True independency is no autonomy from Christ but submission to Him above every earthly power; the same congregation that bows to no pope must bow wholly to her King and walk in love and accountability with other true churches. To recover the doctrine rightly is to prize the local church’s dignity under Christ while refusing both the tyranny of human hierarchy and the disorder of an independence that answers to no one, not even to the Word.
roots_summary: Independent polity roots in Christ’s sole headship and the competence He gives each local church under His Word.
roots_lines: Each local church is a complete, self-governing body under Christ.
No bishop, synod, or pope holds binding jurisdiction over her.
Final discipline rests with the congregation and her Lord.
Churches walk in voluntary fellowship and counsel without surrendering autonomy.
The 1689 Confession sets forth this congregational independency.
usage: “Independent polity confesses no head over the local church but Christ.”
“The Baptists held an independency that rejected prelacy and the papal claim alike.”
“True independency is submission to Christ, not isolation from His people.”
